blocks.text: That نِسْر [nisr] is today the Arabic name of eagles is also confirmed by Forsskål in Descriptt. Animall. p. 12. But just as the Arabs often take eagles, نِسْر [nisr], and vultures, رخم [rakham], indiscriminately, and attribute to the eagle many things that are proper to the vulture, as Bochart will show at length below in Chapter XXVII, so it is likely that the Hebrews too sometimes confused birds of both kinds and took one for the other. Medieval writers also confuse vultures with eagles, as Jo. Gottl. Schneider observes on Frederick II, De arte venandi cum avibus, p. 52. "Of eagles," says Leo Africanus, Descript. Afr. book 9, ch. 56, "there are various species, differing in their properties, size and colour: the larger are called Nesir in the Arabic idiom." And in ch. 57: Nesir "is the largest of the birds of Africa; in body it exceeds the crane, yet it is shorter in beak, neck and legs." These marks are rather uncertain and fit more than one bird of the eagle kind. This one thing seems certain: the word نسر [nsr] comprehends birds similar to one another but different in species. Alb. Schultens rightly says in his Commentary on Job XXXIX, p. 1136: "See Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, where six kinds of eagles are indicated. The name common to all is נשר, نسر [nsr]. The species noted in Scripture are פרס, the ossifrage, and עזניה, the Melanaetos or Valeria." Therefore I cannot agree with Oedmann [Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 1, ch. 5; fasc. 3, p. 164; and fasc. 5, p. 73], who assigns the name נשר to the bearded vulture alone, although I do not think it should be excluded altogether. But most of what is recorded of the נשר in the sacred books fits the whole kind of eagles and vultures. — Michaelis, in Supplemm. p. 1695, which should be read, inclines more to the eagle; with him may be compared what a certain learned man notes in the Sylloge of observations on Bruce's travels, edited by Hassencamp, p. 161.

For my part I would think that these words refer rather to the fact that birds of the eagle and vulture kind bear a denser covering of feathers than other birds of prey. There is no adequate reason for referring them specifically to the bearded vulture, with Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 73.

Oedmann's opinion, vol. 1, p. 64, is that Micah's words allude to the bald back of the head of the bearded vulture, which the head of one who has shorn his hair in mourning resembles. To the objections raised by J. D. Michaelis in the Bibl. Orient. Nova vol. 3, p. 45 ff., he replied in vol. 3, p. 168 ff. The head of the bearded vulture is seen in an illustration at the end of Part 3 of Oedmann's book.

To Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 73, this passage seems to hint at the shaggy appearance of the bearded vulture, caused by the projecting hair-like feathers on the neck, breast and upper back. I can hardly persuade myself that any particular species of eagle was in the writer's mind.

This fable perhaps originated from what Leo Africanus relates of the Nesir, book 9, ch. 57, p. 511: "It lives a very long life, and we have seen very many featherless from old age: therefore, when their feathers fall out, they return to the nest, as if newly hatched, and are fed by the younger ones."

This very eagle, which he had carefully observed, was described most accurately by Aldrovandi, Ornithol. vol. 1, book 2, p. 112. There, among other things, he says: "The colour of the wings and tail was dusky, the more so the larger the feathers. That of the other, smaller feathers of the whole body was a rusty or chestnut brown," with white spots scattered here and there, few on the back, more on the belly, the roots everywhere white. "The flight feathers of the wings were six on each side, two spans and a palm long, with very firm and hard quills." You see that Bochart, with every right, refers Ezekiel's words to the ἀστερίας [asterias], which is also the χρυσάετος [chrysaetos], the largest of the eagles. But here too Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 74, sees his bearded vulture.
